title: Names of fears.
lede: Twenty-four phobias, from the everyday to the gloriously specific, and the Greek roots that let you work out the rest.

card.title: Names of fears
card.desc: Twenty-four phobias and what they're fears of, with the roots that give them away.

questions.ask: What's the name for this fear?

groups.label: Everyday
groups.note: The table: ordinary things with clinical-sounding names.

groups.label: Usual suspects
groups.note: The ones quizmasters reach for once everyone knows arachnophobia.

groups.label: Guess from the roots
groups.note: Know the Greek root and you can work these out on the night.

items.hook: Greek akron, the peak: as in the Acropolis, the city on the heights.
The agora was the open marketplace where the Greeks gathered.
Alektor is Greek for a cockerel.
One of the few with an English root: bogey, as in bogeyman.
Greek kyon, a dog. The Cynic philosophers got their name from being called dog-like.
Greek glossa, the tongue, as in glossary.
Koumpouni is modern Greek for a button.
Greek mysos, filth.
Greek ophis, a serpent, as in Ophiuchus, the snake-bearer of the night sky.
Greek pogon, a beard.
Greek thalassa, the sea. Xenophon's soldiers cheered “Thalatta! Thalatta!” when they finally saw it.
Greek xanthos, yellow: xanthan gum comes from a yellowish bacterium.

items.fear: Peanut butter sticking to the roof of your mouth
items.hook: Not spiders: Arachis is the peanut's botanical name and butyrum is Latin for butter. Gloriously specific, hence a quiz favourite.
The cruelest joke in the dictionary. Sesquipedalian means “a foot and a half long”, and someone added hippopotamus and monstrous to make it worse.
NO MObile PHOne phobia, coined in a 2008 study for the UK Post Office.
Greek treis (three) + kai (and) + deka (ten). If it's Friday the 13th in particular, that's paraskevidekatriaphobia.
Said to come from the Greek for a stilt-walker. The word only caught on in the 1980s and 90s.
Greek trypa, a hole. Think honeycomb, lotus seed pods or an Aero. Technically an aversion rather than a clinical phobia.
Greek haima, blood, as in haemoglobin.
Greek nekros, a dead body, as in necropolis, a city of the dead.
Greek pyr, fire, as in pyrotechnics and a funeral pyre.
Greek hydor, water. It was also an old name for rabies, because sufferers couldn't bear to swallow.
Greek pan, all, as in panorama: the whole view.
The fear of fear, or of developing a phobia. Phobos was the Greek god of fear.
